talks.title: RomHack 2025 - James “albinowax” Kettle - HTTP/1.1 Must Die! The Desync Endgame
talks.teaser: Explores romHack 2025 - James “albinowax” Kettle - HTTP/1.1 Must Die! The Desync Endgame and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
HTTP/1.1 Desync Endgame

James Kettle revisits four years of HTTP request-smuggling research expecting minor edge cases, but finds the problem worsening. HTTP/1.1 cannot reliably separate requests; tiny parser differences between frontends and backends enable desyncs and often full site takeover.

Industry Response vs Reality

Deploying HTTP/2 upstream was the hoped-for fix, yet many stacks accept H2 from clients then downgrade to H1 toward backends. Vendors added regex blocks that stop scanners and classic probes while leaving vulnerabilities exploitable—creating false confidence Kettle calls the “desync endgame.”

Cloudflare Case Study

A researcher’s smuggling test appeared blocked at Cloudflare’s cache edge yet still desynced inside Cloudflare infrastructure, potentially affecting masses of sites when static GET requests omitted cache busters. Kettle argues proxy chains that convert H2→H1→H2 amplify complexity built on a broken foundation.

Research Agenda

He plans new tooling, additional desync attack classes, and scrutiny of whether H2 truly succeeds H1—arguing upstream HTTP/1.1 must die and be proven insecure to drive change.

talks.title: RomHack 2025 - Denis Nagayuk (diversenok) - Attacking Assumptions Behind the Image Load Callbacks
talks.teaser: Examines romHack 2025 - Denis Nagayuk (diversenok) - Attacking Assumptions Behind the Image Load Callbacks and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Feature Overview

Denis Nagayuk (diversenok) of Hunt & Hackett examines Windows image-load notify routines used by Sysmon event 7, AV, and EDR tools to inspect DLL loads and enforce code-signing policies such as System Informer protections.

Callback Semantics

Drivers register via documented APIs receiving mapped image base, process ID, file name, and extended file-object pointers. Callbacks run synchronously after NtMapViewOfSection—post-operation—so images are visible to other threads while inspection runs; drivers cannot cancel loads cleanly without crashing callers.

Scope and Assumptions

The mechanism covers image-backed sections, not all executable private memory or data sections, which drives manual mapping evasion. Nagayuk formalizes OS and driver assumptions: files still exist, names remain queryable, and security products can open or hash images during callbacks.

Research Direction

He maps the file → file object → section → mapped image chain where mismatches create attack surface, aiming to violate those assumptions and show defenders where reliance on image-load callbacks breaks down.

talks.title: RomHack 2025 - Leon Jacobs - 7 Vulns in 7 Days: Breaking Bloatware Faster Than It’s Built
talks.teaser: Reviews romHack 2025 - Leon Jacobs - 7 Vulns in 7 Days: Breaking Bloatware Faster Than Its Built and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Bloatware research origin

Leon Jacobs recounts discovering ASUS DriverHub's local web server after a suspiciously fast reboot during gaming. He targeted ASUS DriverHub, MSI Center, Acer Control Center, and Razer Synapse 4—now patched—using Process Explorer, Binary Ninja, and Burp in VMs with installer anti-VM checks bypassed.

ASUS DriverHub attack path

ADU.exe listens on TCP 5300; the public site's JavaScript calls localhost APIs. Origin-header checks and POST body requirements were reverse-engineered from logs and minified JS, enabling unauthenticated reboot via /reboot with forged origin and JSON command payloads—a string-contains origin-validation flaw.

Broader pattern

Jacobs shows how OEM driver hub bloatware exposes privileged local HTTP APIs to browser-origin policies that are trivially bypassed. The week-long sprint yielded multiple CVEs across vendors, illustrating systemic risk in preinstalled manufacturer utilities that bridge web UIs to system-level actions.

talks.title: RomHack 2025 - Philippe Caturegli
talks.teaser: Evaluates romHack 2025 - Philippe Caturegli and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Domain Collisions Still Matter

Philippe Caturegli presents red-team research on domain name collisions—cases where internal corporate names collide with real, publicly registered TLDs. Despite ICANN studies dating to 2013, enterprises still suffer from choices made decades ago.

## WPAD Gone Wrong

During an IT services engagement, his team registered initech.lc, mirroring a fictional internal domain. Remote employees' browsers queried WPAD URLs like wpad.initech.lc through public DNS when home routers could not resolve internal names, letting attackers host malicious proxy configs.

## Internal AD Names vs. New gTLDs

Many organizations adopted short internal domains before new gTLDs existed. Active Directory cannot rename domains, leaving companies stuck with names now owned by strangers—enabling phishing, credential interception, and VPN bypass scenarios.

## ICANN Mitigations and Gaps

Caturegli reviews ICANN's name collision framework from JAS Global Advisors and discusses newer TLD quirks (including memorable examples like .zip). Defenders should audit internal namespaces, disable unsafe WPAD, and plan migrations where collisions create external trust boundaries.

talks.title: RomHack 2025 - Dr Nestori Syynimaa - The Ultimate Guide for Protecting Hybrid Identities in Entra ID
talks.teaser: Analyzes romHack 2025 - Dr Nestori Syynimaa - The Ultimate Guide for Protecting Hybrid Identities in Entra ID and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Dr. Nestori Syynimaa explores attack paths and defense mechanisms surrounding hybrid identities bridging on-premises Active Directory environments and Entra ID (formerly Azure AD). While Microsoft's 2024 threat intelligence indicates that 99% of observed attacks are password-based, the remaining <1%—representing infrastructure compromise—poses a critical threat because attackers breaching on-premises hybrid components can log in directly as trusted entities. Grounded in graph theory and the tenet that "defenders think in lists, attackers think in graphs," the talk models the trust relationships, stored credentials, and exploitation techniques across five core hybrid architectures, providing concrete administrative mitigations.

### Key Topics
The session analyzes five primary hybrid authentication and synchronization architectures:
1. **Entra Connect Sync**: Examining the exposure of synchronized accounts, administrative web service protocols, and the risks of credential extraction.
2. **Entra Cloud Sync**: Evaluating the lightweight provisioning agent model, certificate-based authentication, and bootstrap renewal mechanisms.
3. **Pass-through Authentication (PTA)**: Assessing agent-based authentication validation against on-premises Active Directory.
4. **Federated Identity (ADFS)**: Dissecting token-signing certificates, trust exploitation, and cross-domain token manipulation.
5. **Exchange Hybrid**: Reviewing service principals, actor tokens, offline impersonation tokens, and Exchange Web Services access.

### Technical Details
- **Entra Connect Sync**: Connect synchronizes on-prem objects to Entra ID using either a user account or an application identity. If an attacker gains local administrator access, they can extract the synchronization credentials (demonstrated live using Syynimaa's `AADInternals` toolkit via `Get-AADIntSyncCredentials`). When application certificates are stored on disk, admins can read the private key. Storing private keys in TPM/HSM restricts signing to the host; however, research from SpecterOps (Daniel Heinsen) revealed that an attacker with local signing privileges can add a new credential to the cloud application to gain persistent offline access. Attackers with synchronization secret access can also exploit soft-match and hard-match features in the Admin Web Service (AWS) to convert cloud-only objects into synchronized objects, enabling unauthorized password resets.
- **Entra Cloud Sync & Pass-Through Authentication (PTA)**: Cloud Sync and PTA utilize an on-premises provisioning agent authenticated via certificate-based authentication to the hybrid identity service. The certificate (valid for roughly 90 days) is automatically renewed via an on-premises bootstrap service every 10 minutes. If compromised, an attacker can contact the bootstrap service offline to renew certificates. Deleting the agent locally leaves cloud records intact; tenant administrators must disable the sync user account, disable PTA in the cloud, or contact Microsoft support to remove lingering agents (which otherwise remain active for up to 10 days of inactivity).
- **ADFS & Federated Identity**: Entra ID trusts authentication tokens signed by the identity provider's certificate based on the `ImmutableID`. Default managed certificates are stored in configuration databases and encrypted, but can be decrypted by local administrators using tools like `AADInternals` (`Export-AADIntAdfsCredentials`). An attacker who acquires the signing certificate can forge tokens for any user across federated or even managed domains within the tenant if immutable ID validation matches without strict domain trust constraints. Storing custom certificates in a Hardware Security Module (HSM) prevents private key export.
- **Exchange Hybrid**: Exchange Hybrid relies on credentials attached to the Office 365 Exchange Online service principal. Compromising the local Exchange server allows administrators to obtain an *actor token*. Attackers can subsequently generate an offline *impersonation token* containing the actor token to impersonate any user (including Global Admins) via Exchange Web Services (EWS).

### Takeaways
- **Tier 0 Designation**: All servers hosting hybrid identity components (Entra Connect, Cloud Sync agents, PTA agents, ADFS, and Exchange Hybrid) must be treated and protected with the same rigor as Tier 0 assets (like Domain Controllers).
- **Credential & Key Protection**: Shift away from user credentials to application-based identities. Where certificates are utilized, use custom certificates stored securely in TPM or HSM to limit offline export.
- **Feature Hardening**: Disable soft matching and hard matching unless actively migrating users to prevent cloud object takeover.
- **Exchange Migration**: Transition away from legacy shared Exchange Online identities to dedicated Exchange Hybrid application identities, and restrict trust settings across federated domains.
